subject: mathematics
title: Fractions · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: compare fractions and calculate with a common denominator.

A fraction represents a number using a numerator and a non-zero denominator. The denominator identifies the number of equal parts in the chosen whole. The numerator counts how many of those parts are being considered. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number creates an equivalent fraction. Adding fractions with different denominators first requires a common denominator. Simplifying a fraction removes a common factor without changing its value.

Worked example / discussion
To add 1/3 and 1/6, rewrite 1/3 as 2/6. Then 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. The parts must refer to the same sized whole.

Practice
Find 3/4 + 1/8, then explain why adding the denominators would be incorrect. Check your result with a diagram divided into equal parts.

subject: general
title: Mixtures · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: choose a separation method using a physical property.

A mixture contains substances combined without all of them forming a new chemical substance. An insoluble solid can be separated from a liquid by filtration. Particles that pass through a filter remain in the collected filtrate. Material trapped by the filter is called the residue. Dissolved salt passes through ordinary filter paper together with the solvent. Evaporation can recover a dissolved solid when the substance and heating conditions are suitable.

Worked example / discussion
Filtering a mixture of sand and water leaves sand as residue. Filtering salt water does not remove the dissolved salt. Choose the method from the properties, rather than the appearance alone.

Practice
Explain a possible sequence for separating sand from a mixture of sand, salt and water. This is a planning activity: practical heating and chemicals require teacher supervision.

subject: agriculture
title: Controlling Soil Pollution · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: identify soil pollution and explain practical prevention.

Soil pollution occurs when harmful substances contaminate the soil environment. Poorly discarded plastics can interfere with cultivation and soil organisms. Uncontrolled dumping can introduce harmful substances into water and farmland. Sorting household waste supports safer reuse, recycling and disposal. Suitable uncontaminated plant material can be managed through composting. Agricultural chemicals must be stored and used according to approved instructions.

Worked example / discussion
Compare a clean garden bed with a nearby littered area without touching unknown waste. Record visible evidence and suggest how the waste could have reached each place.

Practice
Prepare a simple school waste map showing bins, drains and gardens. Recommend ways to prevent pollution. Do not handle sharp objects, unknown containers or chemicals; report them to an adult.

subject: english
title: Listening for Main Idea · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: distinguish the main idea from supporting details.

The main idea expresses the central message of a spoken passage. Supporting details provide examples or explanations that develop that message. Repeated words can help a listener notice the speaker’s central theme. A title can suggest a topic but does not always express the complete meaning. Brief notes help the listener retain important information from the presentation. A useful summary expresses the main message without copying every sentence.

Worked example / discussion
If a speaker describes planting trees, caring for seedlings and protecting forests, the central message may concern tree conservation. A detail such as the number of seedlings supports that message.

Practice
Listen to a short teacher-selected passage. Write one sentence stating the main idea and two details supporting it. Compare answers and identify the evidence behind each choice.

subject: mathematics
title: Rates, Ratio, Proportions and Percentages · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: represent comparisons and calculate percentages.

A ratio compares quantities using an agreed order. Equivalent ratios are formed by multiplying or dividing all terms by the same positive factor. Quantities in a ratio must use compatible units before simplification. A percentage describes a quantity as a fraction with denominator one hundred. A rate compares quantities that may have different measurement units. Direct proportion means one quantity changes by the same factor as another.

Worked example / discussion
For a mixture ratio of 2:3 with 25 parts altogether, there are 5 equal ratio units. Each unit represents 5 parts, so the quantities are 10 and 15. Twenty percent of 150 is 0.20 × 150 = 30.

Practice
A class has 12 learners in one group and 18 in another. Simplify the ratio and express the first group as a percentage of the total. Explain the order used.

subject: general
title: The Cell · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: relate basic cell structures to their functions.

A cell is a basic structural unit of a living organism. The cell membrane controls the passage of substances into and out of the cell. Many cellular reactions occur in the cytoplasm. The nucleus of a typical eukaryotic cell contains genetic information. A plant cell wall provides support outside the cell membrane. Chloroplasts in photosynthetic plant cells contain chlorophyll for absorbing light.

Worked example / discussion
Compare a typical plant-cell diagram with a typical animal-cell diagram. Identify shared structures before describing differences. A simplified diagram does not show every feature of every cell.

Practice
Draw and label both diagrams, then explain one function of each labelled part. Use prepared images or teacher-approved slides; do not collect body samples.

subject: agriculture
title: Soil Conservation Measures · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: explain how soil cover and slope management reduce erosion.

Soil erosion involves the removal and transport of soil particles. Moving water can carry exposed particles away from a field. Wind can remove dry particles from an unprotected soil surface. Vegetation roots help bind the soil and provide protective cover. Mulching covers the surface and can reduce the impact of rainfall. Contour-based practices can slow runoff when correctly designed for the landscape.

Worked example / discussion
Compare pictures of a bare slope and a covered slope after rainfall. Identify visible channels or deposits as evidence of erosion. Do not assume that every difference has a single cause.

Practice
Plan a small supervised comparison using shallow trays of bare and covered soil. Keep the amount of water and slope similar. Record observations and suggest a conservation measure appropriate to the school garden.

subject: english
title: Conversational skills – disagreeing politely · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: express a different view while keeping discussion respectful.

Polite disagreement addresses an idea without attacking the other speaker. Active listening helps a listener understand the claim before responding. A respectful response can acknowledge a useful point before presenting a different opinion. Reasons and examples make a disagreement more helpful than a simple contradiction. Turn-taking gives different speakers a fair opportunity to contribute. Clarifying questions can reveal a misunderstanding in the discussion.

Worked example / discussion
Instead of saying “You know nothing,” try “I see your point about cost, but I think safety also matters because…” The response challenges the idea while showing respect.

Practice
In pairs, discuss whether a school should plant flowers or food crops in a small garden. Give a reason, listen to the reply and disagree politely where necessary.

subject: mathematics
title: Matrices · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: read matrix dimensions and perform compatible addition.

A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of entries in rows and columns. Its order records the number of rows followed by the number of columns. A two-row, three-column matrix therefore has order 2 × 3. Adding matrices requires both matrices to have the same order. Matrix addition combines entries in corresponding positions. Multiplying a matrix by a scalar multiplies each entry by that number.

Worked example / discussion
For A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]], A + B = [[6,8],[10,12]]. The top-left result comes from 1 + 5. This is entry-by-entry addition, not matrix multiplication.

Practice
Write a 2 × 3 matrix representing two shops and three product quantities. Explain the meaning of each row and column. Create a compatible second matrix and find the sum.

subject: general
title: Nutrition in plants · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: explain the requirements and products of photosynthesis.

Photosynthesis uses light energy to form organic food from carbon dioxide and water. Chlorophyll in photosynthetic cells absorbs light used in this process. Water is supplied to the plant through its roots and transport tissues. Carbon dioxide enters leaves through openings called stomata. Oxygen is released as a product of photosynthesis. Light availability and other environmental conditions can limit the rate of the process.

Worked example / discussion
A word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light energy and chlorophyll involved. Plants also carry out respiration, so photosynthesis does not replace all other energy processes.

Practice
Explain why a leaf needs both an effective light-absorbing surface and access to gases. Interpret teacher-provided data comparing photosynthesis under different light levels. Chemical leaf tests require supervised practical work.

subject: agriculture
title: Integrated Farming · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: describe useful links among different farm enterprises.

Integrated farming connects two or more farm activities within one management system. Crop residues may become feed or compost when they are suitable and safe. Properly managed livestock manure can contribute nutrients to crop production. Crop diversity can spread production risks across different farm enterprises. Resource recycling reduces waste but does not remove the need for careful planning. Good hygiene is necessary to prevent contamination within the system.

Worked example / discussion
A school garden may supply vegetable residues for suitable composting, while mature compost supports future crops. This link still requires attention to pests, safe materials and appropriate handling.

Practice
Draw a flow diagram linking crops, livestock, water and organic waste on an example farm. Explain two benefits and two possible risks. Do not assume all residues are safe animal feed.

subject: english
title: Reading for information and meaning · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: locate evidence and distinguish stated meaning from inference.

Skimming helps a reader gain an overview of the whole text. Scanning helps a reader locate a particular detail or keyword. Explicit information is stated directly in the written passage. An inference combines textual evidence with reasonable interpretation. Context can help a reader work out an unfamiliar word’s meaning. A supported answer refers to relevant evidence rather than an unrelated opinion.

Worked example / discussion
If a passage states that the ground was wet and people carried umbrellas, rain is a reasonable inference. The precise time the rain began cannot be known unless the text provides more evidence.

Practice
Read a short teacher-selected article. Identify three stated facts, one inference and the words supporting it. Explain the difference between what the text says and what you conclude.

subject: core-mathematics
title: Indices and Logarithms · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: connect powers and logarithms using valid conditions.

An index indicates how many factors of a base occur in a positive integer power. Multiplying powers with the same non-zero base involves adding their indices. Dividing powers with the same non-zero base involves subtracting their indices. A logarithm answers the question of which exponent produces a given positive number. A real logarithm requires a positive base different from one. The argument of a real logarithm must also be positive.

Worked example / discussion
Since 2³ = 8, log base 2 of 8 equals 3. Also 3² × 3⁴ = 3⁶. These rules apply to the same base; they do not mean that 2² + 2³ equals 2⁵.

Practice
Evaluate 5² × 5³ and write 10³ = 1000 in logarithmic form. Explain why log base 10 of zero has no real value.

subject: biology
title: Chemicals of life · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: connect major biological molecules with their roles.

Carbohydrates include simple sugars and larger molecules such as starch. Proteins are built from smaller units called amino acids. Enzymes are biological catalysts, and most enzymes are proteins. Lipids include substances important in energy storage and cell membranes. Nucleic acids contain information used in inheritance and protein production. Water provides a medium for many reactions and movement of dissolved substances.

Worked example / discussion
Compare the roles of starch as a storage carbohydrate and an enzyme as a reaction catalyst. Both occur in living systems, but their structures and functions differ.

Practice
Make a table linking carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids and water to one function each. Explain why identifying a food as containing one nutrient does not mean it contains no others. Laboratory food tests require teacher supervision.

subject: chemistry
title: The Atom · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: relate atomic particles to identity and charge.

An atom has a small nucleus containing protons and, in most atoms, neutrons. Electrons occupy regions outside the nucleus rather than fixed miniature planetary tracks. The proton number identifies which chemical element the atom belongs to. A neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons. Isotopes of an element have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. An ion forms when an atom or group gains or loses electrons.

Worked example / discussion
An atom with 11 protons is sodium. A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons. If it loses one electron, it has a charge of +1; its proton number has not changed.

Practice
Compare atoms with 6 protons and either 6 or 8 neutrons. Explain why they are isotopes of the same element. Distinguish atomic mass number from a relative atomic mass average.

subject: core-mathematics
title: Sequences and Series · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: identify arithmetic and geometric patterns.

A sequence is an ordered list of terms following a stated rule. A series is formed by adding terms from a sequence. An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference between consecutive terms. A geometric sequence has a constant ratio between consecutive terms. The nth term of an arithmetic sequence is a + (n − 1)d. The nth term of a geometric sequence is ar^(n − 1).

Worked example / discussion
The sequence 3, 7, 11, 15 has first term 3 and common difference 4. Its tenth term is 3 + 9 × 4 = 39. The sequence 2, 6, 18 has common ratio 3.

Practice
Find the first five terms when a = 5 and d = −2. Then find the sixth term of a geometric sequence with a = 4 and r = 2. Explain how a series differs from its underlying sequence.

subject: biology
title: Ecology · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: interpret population change using ecological factors.

A population contains organisms of the same species in a defined area. A community contains the different populations living in the same area. Births and immigration can increase the size of a population. Deaths and emigration can reduce the number of individuals present. Limiting factors restrict growth when resources or conditions become less favourable. Carrying capacity describes the population an environment can support under particular conditions.

Worked example / discussion
A population starts with 100 individuals. There are 20 births, 8 deaths, 5 immigrants and 7 emigrants. Its new size is 100 + 20 − 8 + 5 − 7 = 110, assuming those figures describe the same interval.

Practice
Interpret a population graph that rises quickly before levelling off. Suggest two limiting factors and explain why the graph alone does not prove which factor caused the change.

subject: chemistry
title: Reaction Rates · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: explain collision-based factors affecting reaction speed.

Reaction rate measures how quickly reactants are used or products are formed. Collisions must involve sufficient energy and appropriate orientation for a reaction. Higher temperature usually increases reaction rate by changing collision frequency and energy. Greater concentration can increase collision frequency in a suitable reacting solution. Smaller pieces of a solid expose a larger total surface area. A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

Worked example / discussion
For a suitable solid–solution reaction, small particles can react faster than the same mass in a large piece. The comparison is fair only when other relevant conditions are controlled.

Practice
Plan how to compare rates using teacher-provided data for different temperatures. Name the independent, dependent and control variables. Practical reactions need teacher-approved chemicals, apparatus and supervision.

subject: essential-mathematics
title: Sets · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: use set notation and interpret intersections and unions.

A set is a collection whose membership can be clearly determined. A universal set defines the objects under consideration in a problem. The intersection of two sets contains the elements belonging to both sets. The union contains elements belonging to either set, counting each element once. The complement contains elements in the universal set that are outside the chosen set. A Venn diagram represents relationships between sets using regions.

Worked example / discussion
If A = {1,2,3} and B = {3,4}, then A ∩ B = {3} and A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4}. If U = {1,2,3,4,5}, the complement of A is {4,5}.

Practice
In a group of 30 learners, 18 study one activity, 15 study another and 7 study both. Find how many study at least one and how many study neither. State the universal set.

subject: chemistry
title: Polymers · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: relate monomers, polymer chains and material properties.

A polymer is a large molecule containing many repeating structural units. Smaller starting molecules used to produce polymers are called monomers. Addition polymerisation can join suitable unsaturated monomers without producing a small-molecule by-product. Condensation polymerisation links suitable functional groups and releases small molecules. Chain structure and bonding help explain differences in polymer properties. Some polymers occur naturally while others are made through industrial processes.

Worked example / discussion
Poly(ethene) forms when many ethene molecules join through addition polymerisation. Cellulose is an example of a naturally occurring polymer. A material’s properties depend on more than the length of its chains alone.

Practice
Compare addition and condensation polymerisation using a teacher-approved diagram. Explain why identifying a plastic does not establish whether it is biodegradable or locally recyclable. Use correct local waste-disposal guidance; do not burn plastics.

subject: physics
title: Electromagnetic induction · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: explain the conditions for an induced potential difference.

Electromagnetic induction can produce an electromotive force when magnetic flux linkage changes. Moving a magnet relative to a coil can change the flux through the coil. Faster change of flux linkage produces a larger induced electromotive force. A greater number of turns can increase the effect under comparable conditions. The direction of induced current opposes the change producing it, according to Lenz’s law. A current flows only when the conducting circuit is complete.

Worked example / discussion
A coil connected to a sensitive meter gives a deflection when a nearby magnet moves relative to it. Reversing the motion reverses the deflection. A stationary arrangement with constant flux does not maintain an induced electromotive force.

Practice
Explain how changing motion, coil turns and magnetic field strength could affect an observation. Interpret a teacher demonstration or simulation. Do not experiment with mains electricity.

subject: mathematics
title: Quadratic Expressions and Equations II · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: solve a quadratic and check its roots.

A quadratic equation can be written as ax² + bx + c = 0 with a non-zero coefficient a. Factoring expresses a quadratic as a product when suitable factors exist. The zero-product rule states that a product is zero only if at least one factor is zero. The quadratic formula gives roots as [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/(2a). The discriminant b² − 4ac indicates the nature of real roots. Substitution into the original equation provides a useful final check.

Worked example / discussion
For x² − 5x + 6 = 0, factor to obtain (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. Therefore x = 2 or x = 3. Both values satisfy the original equation.

Practice
Solve 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0 by factorisation and verify both roots. Explain why dividing an equation by an expression that might be zero can lose a solution.

subject: biology
title: Ecology · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: trace energy transfer and interpret feeding relationships.

An ecosystem includes living organisms and the physical conditions surrounding them. Producers build organic food using an energy source such as sunlight. Consumers obtain organic food by feeding on other organisms. Decomposers help break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the environment. Food-chain arrows indicate the direction of energy transfer from food to consumer. A food web combines several linked feeding relationships.

Worked example / discussion
Grass → grasshopper → frog represents one possible food chain. The arrow points from grass to grasshopper because feeding transfers energy in that direction. Real ecosystems contain many additional feeding links.

Practice
Draw a food web using a suitable local or textbook example. Explain how removal of one organism might affect several populations. Distinguish nutrient recycling from energy transfer; energy is not recycled around the ecosystem in the same way.

subject: physics
title: Linear Motion · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement and depth. Supplementary notes, not the complete official syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: distinguish displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.

Distance is the total length of the path travelled by an object. Displacement measures the change of position with a specified direction. Average speed equals total distance divided by the total elapsed time. Average velocity uses displacement divided by the same time interval. Acceleration measures the change in velocity per unit time. Uniform acceleration allows the use of equations such as v = u + at.

Worked example / discussion
A learner walks 30 m east and then 10 m west in 20 s. Distance is 40 m and displacement is 20 m east. Average speed is 2 m/s; average velocity is 1 m/s east.

Practice
An object changes velocity from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s along a straight line. Calculate its average acceleration. State when speed can be non-zero while displacement is zero.

subject: mathematics
title: Factors · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: identify factors and use common factors to simplify a fraction.

A factor divides a whole number exactly without leaving a remainder. A multiple is obtained by multiplying a number by a whole number. The highest common factor is the greatest factor shared by the chosen positive integers. The lowest common multiple is the smallest positive multiple shared by those integers. A prime number has exactly two positive factors, itself and one. Prime factorisation expresses a positive integer greater than one as a product of prime factors.

Worked example / discussion
The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. The factors of 18 include 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. Their highest common factor is 6, so 12/18 simplifies to 2/3.

Practice
List the factors of 20 and 30. Find their highest common factor and lowest common multiple. Answers: 10 and 60.

subject: mathematics
title: Linear Equations · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: solve an equation and verify the answer by substitution.

An equation states that two expressions have the same value. A variable represents an unknown number in the equation. Adding or subtracting the same quantity on both sides preserves equality. Multiplying or dividing both sides by the same non-zero number also preserves equality. Like terms contain the same variable raised to the same power. Substitution checks a proposed solution by replacing the variable with its numerical value.

Worked example / discussion
For 3x + 5 = 20, subtract 5 from both sides to obtain 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 5. Substitution gives 3(5) + 5 = 20.

Practice
Solve 2x - 4 = 10 and check your answer. Answer: x = 7.

subject: mathematics
title: Integers · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: calculate with positive and negative integers.

Integers include positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers and zero. A number line places negative integers to the left of zero and positive integers to the right. Opposite integers have equal distances from zero but opposite signs. Adding a negative number moves a position to the left on the number line. Subtracting a number is equivalent to adding its opposite. The product of two integers with unlike signs is negative, while the product of two negative integers is positive.

Worked example / discussion
For -3 + 7, begin at -3 and move seven places right to reach 4. For 5 - (-2), add the opposite of -2: 5 + 2 = 7.

Practice
Calculate -8 + 3, -4 x 6 and -12 / -3. Answers: -5, -24 and 4.

subject: mathematics
title: Probability · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: describe equally likely outcomes and calculate a simple probability.

An outcome is a possible result of a chance experiment. A sample space lists all possible outcomes for the experiment. An event is a collection of outcomes with a stated property. For equally likely outcomes, probability equals the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. A probability lies between zero and one, inclusive. The probability of an event not occurring is one minus the probability of that event occurring.

Worked example / discussion
A fair six-sided die has six equally likely outcomes. The even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6, so the probability of an even result is 3/6 = 1/2.

Practice
Find the probability of rolling a number greater than four on a fair six-sided die. Answer: 2/6 = 1/3. Explain why the die must be fair for this calculation.

subject: mathematics
title: Cubes and Cube Roots · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: calculate cubes and recognise exact cube roots.

The cube of a number is the product of three equal factors of that number. A cube root reverses the operation of cubing. A perfect cube of an integer has an integer cube root. Cubing a negative number produces a negative result because three negative factors have a negative product. In prime factorisation of a positive perfect cube, each prime exponent is a multiple of three. A cube with edge length measured in centimetres has its volume measured in cubic centimetres.

Worked example / discussion
The cube of 4 is 4 x 4 x 4 = 64, so the cube root of 64 is 4. A cube with an edge of 3 cm has a volume of 27 cubic centimetres.

Practice
Calculate the cube of -3 and the cube root of 125. Answers: -27 and 5.

subject: mathematics
title: Mass, Volume, Weight, and Density · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: distinguish mass from weight and calculate density with consistent units.

Mass measures the amount of matter in an object and is commonly measured in kilograms. Volume measures the space occupied by an object or substance. Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object and is measured in newtons. Density is mass divided by volume when both quantities use consistent units. A density in grams per cubic centimetre uses mass in grams and volume in cubic centimetres. Converting units before calculating helps prevent incorrect numerical comparisons.

Worked example / discussion
A sample has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 40 cubic centimetres. Its density is 120 / 40 = 3 g per cubic centimetre.

Practice
Find the density of a 250 g object occupying 50 cubic centimetres. Answer: 5 g per cubic centimetre. Explain why kilograms and newtons are not interchangeable.

subject: general
title: Laboratory Safety · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: recognise hazards and follow teacher-approved laboratory procedures.

A hazard is a possible source of harm during an activity. A risk depends on the likelihood and consequences of that harm. Protective equipment reduces exposure but does not remove the need for careful procedures. A container label helps identify its contents and the precautions needed for handling. A clear work area reduces accidental contact with equipment and materials. A damaged instrument should be reported rather than used in a practical activity.

Worked example / discussion
Before a practical, identify the equipment, read the teacher's instructions and point out the emergency exit. Tell the teacher immediately about a spill or breakage. Keep food and drinks outside the laboratory.

Practice
Identify two hazards in a crowded workbench drawing and suggest a safer arrangement. Never taste substances, smell them directly or handle an unknown chemical; wait for teacher guidance.

subject: general
title: Electrical Energy · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: explain why a simple low-voltage circuit needs a complete path.

A simple electric circuit needs a complete conducting path for a steady current to flow. A cell transfers energy to the circuit and has positive and negative terminals. A closed switch completes a conducting connection within the circuit. An open switch interrupts the conducting path and stops the current in a simple circuit. A conductor allows electric charge to move more readily than an insulator. A bulb transfers electrical energy into light and thermal energy during operation.

Worked example / discussion
In a diagram containing one cell, one bulb and a switch, trace the path from one cell terminal through the components to the other terminal. Predict what happens when the switch opens.

Practice
Explain why a bulb will not light if a connecting wire is missing. Use a simulation for independent work. Physical circuits require teacher-approved low-voltage supplies; never use mains electricity.

subject: general
title: Physical and chemical changes · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: use observations to distinguish types of change.

A physical change alters a state or physical property without creating a new substance. A chemical change produces substances with different chemical compositions. Melting changes a solid into a liquid without necessarily changing its chemical identity. Observations such as gas formation or a temperature change can provide evidence of a reaction but need interpretation. Reversibility alone is not a reliable test for deciding whether a change is chemical. A scientific conclusion connects the observations to an explanation rather than relying on appearance alone.

Worked example / discussion
Compare ice melting with an iron object rusting. Melted pure water remains water, while rusting produces new iron-containing substances. Use prepared pictures and descriptions rather than carrying out an unsupervised reaction.

Practice
Classify cutting paper and burning paper. Explain the role of new substances in your decision. Cutting is physical; burning is chemical. Heating and burning require teacher supervision.

subject: general
title: Pressure · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: relate pressure to force and contact area.

Pressure is the normal force acting per unit area on a surface. A normal force acts perpendicular to the surface being considered. For a fixed force, increasing the contact area decreases pressure. For a fixed area, increasing the force increases pressure. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, equivalent to one newton per square metre. Comparing pressures requires both force and area to be expressed in compatible units.

Worked example / discussion
A force of 60 N acts normally on an area of 3 square metres. The pressure is 60 / 3 = 20 Pa. If the same force acts on 6 square metres, the pressure becomes 10 Pa.

Practice
Calculate the pressure from 100 N acting on 2 square metres. Answer: 50 Pa. Explain why a wide support spreads a load. Use diagrams or safe classroom models; do not test with sharp objects.

title: Structure of the atom · Revision notes
author: JEZTECH original revision resource
review: Teacher review required for class placement, accuracy and depth. Supplementary explanation, not an official KICD document or the complete syllabus.
content:
Learning goal: describe the basic particles of an atom and its electrical neutrality.

An atom has a small nucleus containing protons and, for most atoms, neutrons. A proton has a positive electrical charge and an electron has a negative electrical charge. A neutron has no net electrical charge. Electrons occupy regions outside the nucleus rather than being fixed inside it. A neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons. The atomic number gives the number of protons in the nucleus and identifies the element.

Worked example / discussion
A neutral atom containing six protons also contains six electrons. If its nucleus contains six neutrons, its mass number is 6 + 6 = 12. A model drawing is a simplified representation and is not drawn to actual scale.

Practice
A neutral atom has eight protons and eight neutrons. State its number of electrons, atomic number and mass number. Answers: 8, 8 and 16.

content:
Learning goal: describe wave features and calculate a simple wave speed.

A wave transfers energy through a disturbance without an overall transfer of the medium over long distances. Wavelength is the distance between consecutive points in the same phase of a wave. Frequency is the number of complete oscillations passing a point each second. The hertz is the unit of frequency and means one cycle per second. Amplitude measures the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position. Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength when compatible units are used.

Worked example / discussion
A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. Its speed is 4 x 2 = 8 m/s. A labelled diagram should distinguish the vertical amplitude from the horizontal wavelength.

Practice
A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and wavelength of 3 m. Calculate its speed. Answer: 15 m/s. Use diagrams or teacher-approved simulations for independent practice.
